questions.stem: A radio wave of frequency 98 MHz reaches a receiving antenna. How do the free electrons in the antenna respond?
options: They flow steadily in one direction along the antenna
They oscillate at a frequency set by the antenna's length alone
They are emitted from the antenna as a beam of particles
They oscillate at 98 MHz, the frequency of the wave
questions.explanation: The oscillating electric field of the wave pushes the antenna's electrons back and forth at the wave's frequency, producing a small alternating current that the receiver detects. A transmitting antenna works the other way: electrons oscillating at a frequency radiate waves of that frequency.

questions.stem: A transmitter uses a vertical antenna, so its waves are vertically polarised. How should a simple rod receiving antenna be orientated for the strongest signal?
options: Horizontally, at right angles to the wave's oscillating electric field
Pointing straight at the transmitter, along the direction of travel
At 45° to the vertical, to receive both polarisations equally
Vertically, parallel to the wave's oscillating electric field
questions.explanation: The receiving rod's electrons are driven along its length by the wave's electric field, which is vertical here. A vertical rod gives the largest oscillation; a horizontal rod, at right angles to the field, receives very little.

questions.stem: Microwaves used in a school demonstration have a wavelength of 3.0 cm. What is their frequency? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options: 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz
questions.explanation: f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸/0.030 = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz, or 10 GHz. Using 3.0 instead of 0.030 m gives 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz; the wavelength must be in metres.

questions.stem: What is monochromatic light?
options: Light that travels in a single direction
Light composed of a single frequency
Light whose waves keep a constant phase relationship
Light that is polarised in a single plane
questions.explanation: Monochromatic means a single frequency, and so a single wavelength in a given medium. A constant phase relationship describes coherence, a separate property.

questions.stem: What does it mean for two light sources to be coherent?
options: Their waves have the same speed in every transparent medium
Their waves maintain a constant phase relationship with each other
Their waves have the same amplitude and travel in the same direction
Their waves are both polarised in the same plane as each other
questions.explanation: Coherent waves keep a fixed phase difference over time. They must have the same frequency to do so. Coherence is needed for a stable interference pattern.

questions.stem: Why is light from an incandescent globe neither coherent nor monochromatic?
options: Its light travels too slowly through the glass to keep a constant phase
Its atoms all emit in step, but at many different amplitudes and speeds
Its atoms emit independently at random times, over a wide range of frequencies
Its filament emits only one frequency, but the glass changes the phase at random
questions.explanation: A hot filament emits a continuous range of frequencies, so it is not monochromatic. Its countless atoms emit independently at random moments, so there is no fixed phase relationship and it is not coherent.

questions.stem: Two wave sources are described as being in phase. What does this mean?
options: They produce waves of the same amplitude
They produce crests at the same instant
They produce crests at the same rate but at different instants
They produce a crest from one as the other produces a trough
questions.explanation: Sources in phase reach their crests and troughs at the same moments. If one produces a crest while the other produces a trough, they are exactly out of phase.

questions.stem: Two light waves of equal amplitude meet at a point exactly out of phase. What is the result there?
options: Destructive interference, with half the original amplitude
No interference, because light waves pass through each other
Destructive interference, with zero resultant amplitude
Constructive interference, with double the amplitude
questions.explanation: By superposition, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements. A crest always meeting a trough of equal size gives zero: complete destructive interference. Light waves do pass through each other, but they superpose where they overlap.

questions.stem: Two monochromatic sources oscillate in phase. At which path differences does constructive interference occur?
options: λ/m, where m is a whole number
2mλ only, where m is a whole number
mλ, where m is a whole number
(m + ½)λ, where m is a whole number
questions.explanation: If the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively. A path difference of (m + ½)λ brings them in exactly out of phase, giving destructive interference.

questions.stem: Two in-phase sources emit light of wavelength 600 nm. A point P is 900 nm further from one source than the other. What happens at P?
options: Constructive interference, because the path difference is 1.5λ
Constructive interference, because 900 nm is more than one wavelength
Destructive interference, because the path difference is 0.67λ
Destructive interference, because the path difference is 1.5λ
questions.explanation: Path difference/λ = 900/600 = 1.5, a whole number plus one-half. The waves arrive exactly out of phase, so P is a point of minimum intensity.

questions.stem: Two light waves, each of amplitude A, meet at a point exactly in phase. What is the resultant amplitude there?
options: 2A
A
A²
questions.explanation: By the principle of superposition the displacements add. In phase, crest meets crest and trough meets trough, so the resultant amplitude is A + A = 2A: constructive interference.

questions.stem: Two microwave transmitters emit the same wavelength but are driven exactly out of phase. What is detected at a point equally distant from both?
options: A minimum, because equal distances always give destructive interference
A minimum, because waves that start out of phase arrive out of phase
A maximum, because the path difference to the point is zero
A maximum, because out-of-phase sources always interfere constructively
questions.explanation: With zero path difference, the waves arrive with the same phase relationship they started with. Here they start exactly out of phase, so they cancel. For in-phase sources the same point would be a maximum.

questions.stem: In Young's double-slit pattern, what is the path difference from the two slits to the third bright fringe from the central maximum?
options: 6λ
3λ
questions.explanation: The central maximum has zero path difference and each further bright fringe adds one wavelength, so the third bright fringe has a path difference of 3λ. 2.5λ corresponds to the third dark fringe.

questions.stem: Why does Young's double-slit experiment support the wave model of light?
options: It produces two bright bands, one directly behind each of the slits
It produces alternating bright and dark fringes, which only interference can explain
It shows light travelling in perfectly straight lines through both slits
It shows that light carries momentum and pushes on the screen
questions.explanation: Particles travelling in straight lines would give two bright bands behind the slits. The many bright and dark fringes are explained by waves from the two slits superposing constructively and destructively.

questions.stem: In a two-slit interference experiment, why must the light diffract at the slits?
options: So the light spreads out from each slit and the two beams overlap
So the light slows down and the two beams have the same speed
So the light from each slit becomes polarised in the same plane
So the light changes frequency to match the slit width
questions.explanation: Each narrow slit diffracts the light, spreading it out. Without this spreading, the beams from the two slits would not overlap on the screen, and there would be no interference pattern.

questions.stem: Why is a laser usually used as the light source for a laboratory double-slit experiment?
options: It gives light of many frequencies, so more fringes appear on the screen
It gives unpolarised light, which diffracts more strongly at the slits
It gives light that travels faster, so the fringes are further apart
It gives coherent, monochromatic light, so a stable, clear pattern forms
questions.explanation: Light from the two slits must keep a constant phase relationship to make a stable pattern, and a single wavelength gives sharp, evenly spaced fringes. A laser's light is coherent and monochromatic.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 633 nm passes through two slits 0.25 mm apart onto a screen 2.0 m away. What is the spacing between adjacent bright fringes?
options: 1.3 mm
51 mm
5.1 mm
questions.explanation: Δy = λL/d = 633 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.0/(0.25 × 10⁻³) = 5.1 × 10⁻³ m = 5.1 mm. Converting 0.25 mm wrongly as 2.5 × 10⁻³ m gives 0.51 mm.

questions.stem: Adjacent bright fringes are 4.0 mm apart on a screen 2.0 m from two slits 0.30 mm apart. What is the wavelength of the light?
questions.explanation: λ = dΔy/L = 0.30 × 10⁻³ × 4.0 × 10⁻³/2.0 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, which is 600 nm, orange light. Measuring across several fringes and dividing reduces the uncertainty in Δy.

questions.stem: The slits in a double-slit experiment are replaced with slits half as far apart. What happens to the fringes?
options: They become half as far apart
They stay the same distance apart
They become four times as far apart
They become twice as far apart
questions.explanation: Δy = λL/d, so the fringe spacing is inversely proportional to the slit separation. Halving d doubles Δy.

questions.stem: Red light in a double-slit experiment is replaced by blue light, with everything else unchanged. What happens to the fringe pattern?
options: The fringes stay in exactly the same places
The pattern disappears completely
The fringes move closer together
The fringes move further apart
questions.explanation: Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, and Δy = λL/d, so the fringe spacing decreases.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through slits 0.20 mm apart. At what angle is the second-order bright fringe?
questions.explanation: d sin θ = mλ, so sin θ = 2 × 500 × 10⁻⁹/(0.20 × 10⁻³) = 5.0 × 10⁻³ and θ = 0.29°. Using m = 1 gives 0.14°. The angles in a double-slit pattern are small, which is why Δy = λL/d works.

questions.stem: How should the intensity graph for two-slit interference of monochromatic light be sketched, when the slit separation is much greater than the slit width?
options: Maxima getting rapidly brighter the further they are from the centre
Very sharp, narrow maxima separated by wide dark regions, like a grating
Equally spaced maxima of about equal intensity, with near-zero minima between
A single broad central maximum with no other bright regions on either side
questions.explanation: Near the centre, two-slit interference gives bright fringes of about equal brightness and spacing, with dark fringes between them where the waves cancel. Very sharp maxima with wide dark gaps are characteristic of a grating with many slits.

questions.stem: What causes a dark fringe in the double-slit pattern?
options: Light being absorbed by the material between the two slits
The shadow of the barrier between the slits falling on the screen
Destructive interference, where the path difference is (m + ½)λ
Constructive interference, where the path difference is mλ
questions.explanation: At a dark fringe, waves from the two slits arrive exactly out of phase because their path difference is a whole number plus one-half of wavelengths, so they cancel.

questions.stem: A double-slit experiment is repeated with the screen moved from 1.5 m to 3.0 m from the slits. What happens to the fringe spacing?
options: It halves
It stays the same
It quadruples
It doubles
questions.explanation: Δy = λL/d, so the spacing is directly proportional to the slit-to-screen distance L. Doubling L doubles Δy, though the fringes also become dimmer.

questions.stem: What is a transmission diffraction grating?
options: A thick glass prism that refracts each colour through a different angle
A single narrow slit that spreads light into a broad central maximum
A pair of polarising filters with their axes set at right angles
A transparent sheet with a very large number of very narrow, equally spaced slits
questions.explanation: A grating has hundreds of parallel slits per millimetre. Light diffracted by the many slits interferes to give bright maxima at angles given by d sin θ = mλ.

questions.stem: In the derivation of d sin θ = mλ for a grating, what does d sin θ represent?
options: The distance from the grating to the screen
The width of each individual slit in the grating
The distance between adjacent maxima on the screen
The path difference between waves from adjacent slits
questions.explanation: Waves leaving adjacent slits at angle θ travel distances that differ by d sin θ. When this equals a whole number of wavelengths, waves from all the slits arrive in phase and a bright maximum forms.

questions.stem: Why does a grating give much sharper and brighter maxima, at much larger angles, than a double slit?
options: The light slows down inside the grating, which makes the maxima narrower
Many slits must all be in phase for a maximum, and the slits are very close together
Each slit in a grating is much wider, so it lets far more light through
A grating refracts the light as well as diffracting it, adding extra brightness
questions.explanation: With many slits, waves from all of them add only at precise angles, so maxima are bright and narrow and are separated by wide dark regions. The very small slit spacing d makes the angles large, since sin θ = mλ/d.

questions.stem: A grating has 600 lines per millimetre. What is the slit spacing d?
questions.explanation: 600 lines per millimetre is 6.0 × 10⁵ lines per metre, so d = 1/(6.0 × 10⁵) = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m. Taking 1/600 without converting to metres gives 1.67 × 10⁻³, which is in millimetres.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 550 nm falls on a grating with 600 lines per millimetre. At what angle is the first-order maximum?
questions.explanation: d = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m, so sin θ = λ/d = 550 × 10⁻⁹/1.67 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.330 and θ = 19.3°. The second order is at 41.3°.

questions.stem: For light of wavelength 550 nm on a grating with 600 lines per millimetre, what is the highest order of maximum that can be observed?
questions.explanation: sin θ cannot exceed 1, so m ≤ d/λ = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶/550 × 10⁻⁹ = 3.03. The highest whole number is 3, so third-order maxima appear on each side but not fourth.

questions.stem: Monochromatic light gives a first-order maximum at 20.0° with a grating of slit spacing 1.60 × 10⁻⁶ m. What is its wavelength?
options: 547 nm
273 nm
584 nm
questions.explanation: λ = d sin θ/m = 1.60 × 10⁻⁶ × sin 20.0° = 5.47 × 10⁻⁷ m = 547 nm. Using cos 20° instead of sin 20° gives 1.50 µm.

questions.stem: How should the intensity graph for monochromatic light through a transmission grating be sketched?
options: A smooth intensity that is the same at every angle from the grating
Narrow, sharp maxima with wide regions of almost zero intensity between
Broad maxima of equal width with narrow dark lines between them
One bright central maximum that fades smoothly to dark on each side
questions.explanation: A grating gives sharply defined, bright maxima at the angles where d sin θ = mλ, separated by broad dark regions. This is what makes accurate angle measurement possible.

questions.stem: White light passes through a grating. What is seen on each side of the central maximum?
options: A series of white maxima, because white light contains all colours
A single spectrum on one side only, as with a prism
A spectrum in each order, with violet nearest the centre and red furthest out
A spectrum in each order, with red nearest the centre and violet furthest out
questions.explanation: The central maximum is white because every wavelength has zero path difference there. In each order, sin θ = mλ/d, so shorter wavelengths, violet, are deviated least and red most.

questions.stem: White light (400-700 nm) falls on a grating with 500 lines per millimetre. Which orders overlap?
options: The second and third orders overlap; the first and second do not
The first and second orders overlap; the second and third do not
No orders overlap, because each order is a separate spectrum
Every order overlaps the next, starting with the first and second
questions.explanation: d = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. First-order red is at sin θ = 0.35 and second-order violet at 0.40, so they are separate. Second-order red is at 0.70 but third-order violet is at 0.60, so these overlap.

questions.stem: Why are transmission gratings rather than double slits used in spectroscopy?
options: They work only with coherent laser light, which is easier to measure accurately
They absorb unwanted wavelengths, so only the strongest spectral line remains
Their maxima are bright, sharp and widely spread, so wavelengths can be measured precisely
They produce light of a single colour, so no spectrum is formed to confuse the reading
questions.explanation: Gratings separate wavelengths through large angles and give sharp, bright lines, so close wavelengths can be told apart and their angles measured accurately. A double slit gives broad, closely spaced fringes.

questions.stem: How can a transmission grating be used to measure the wavelength of a monochromatic source?
options: Measure the brightness of the central maximum and divide by d
Count the slits that the light passes through and multiply by d
Measure the time the light takes to pass through the grating
Measure the angle of a known order and use λ = d sin θ/m
questions.explanation: With the slit spacing d known from the lines per millimetre, measuring the angle θ of the mth-order maximum gives λ = d sin θ/m. Measuring both sides and higher orders improves precision.
